Act as a product designer doing divergent thinking exercises.
Take this problem and starting idea and generate business ideas.
[PROBLEM]
Messenger You Cannot Mute
[STARTING IDEA]
A messaging app or device where every incoming message makes a sound at maximum volume. Users cannot mute notifications or reduce the volume.

Generate 2 diverse problem-solution pairs. For each:
1. The specific problem
2. Why this persona cares
3. A simple solution concept
4. Likelihood this is a real, painful problem (1-10)

Here are two deliberately different directions for “Messenger You Cannot Mute”:

Idea 1 — Critical Operations Messenger
1. Specific problem: On-call workers miss genuinely urgent alerts because critical messages compete with normal notifications. Persona: hospital operations staff, data-center engineers, security teams, building maintenance, incident-response teams.
2. Why this persona cares: Missing one alert can mean an outage lasts longer, equipment gets damaged, a safety issue escalates, or an SLA is violated. They need a channel that is meaningfully different from ordinary Slack/SMS noise.
3. Simple solution concept: Escalation-only messenger. Ordinary messages behave normally, but authorized “critical alerts” override silent mode, sound repeatedly, vibrate, and escalate to another device/person until acknowledged. The system heavily restricts who can trigger these alerts and keeps an audit log to prevent abuse.
4. Likelihood this is a real, painful problem: 9/10. Incident escalation is already a serious category with products like paging/on-call systems, which strongly validates the pain.

Idea 2 — Accountability Messenger
1. Specific problem: People deliberately ignore messages that require uncomfortable but time-sensitive action. Persona: small project teams, student groups, startup founders, or field crews where one ignored message can block everyone else.
2. Why this persona cares: A teammate saying “I didn’t see the message” can delay a submission, handoff, meeting, delivery, or operational task. The sender needs confirmation that the recipient has actually noticed the request.
3. Simple solution concept: Acknowledgment-required messenger. Selected messages remain persistently visible/audible until the recipient explicitly chooses something like “Seen,” “Doing it,” “Need help,” or “Cannot do.” Instead of literally blasting maximum volume indefinitely, the product makes ignoring the task socially and operationally difficult.
4. Likelihood this is a real, painful problem: 7/10. The underlying coordination problem is common, although users may strongly resist a product that removes too much notification control.

The interesting design insight is that “cannot mute” is probably too hostile as a general-purpose messaging feature, but potentially valuable when reframed as either verified urgency or forced acknowledgment. The business opportunity is therefore less “annoying messenger” and more a communication channel whose defining promise is: this message cannot quietly disappear.
